(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Experimental Station of Jilin

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Due to soil erosion, intensive land use, and the removal of straw, resulting in shallow tillage, hard subsurface layers, and poor fertility, the quality and quantity of soil organic carbon (SOC) in arable soils in the black soils of Northeast China have significantly decreased over the past few years.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) In China, returning straw to the field is a common practice as straw consists of nearly all of the carbon (C) absorbed from the soil.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The continuous application, slow decomposition, and retention of straw, however, may impede tillage and crop growth and also nutrient effectiveness, soil temperature, water infiltration and evaporation, and pest and disease populations.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) According to studies, the contents of the straw and the method of application have an impact on the rate that it breaks down in the soil.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) By altering microbial colonization  , co-metabolism  , or mineral catalysis  , the straw interaction with soil promotes straw decomposition.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Thus, the depth and positioning of crop straw may affect the rate at which it decomposes.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Furthermore, the application of straw is critical to the division and mineralization of straw as these are both key to the efficient use of straw.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) To place crop straw in contact with the soil at various depths, it can either be left on the ground as mulch or combined into the soil by tilling, rototilling, or disk tilling.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The composition of agricultural straw is mainly affected by its C content, N concentration, C/N ratio, and lignin content.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Based on studies conducted by Gaind and Nain (2007) , the crop straw's lignin amount may be considered a valid indicator of the rate at which the straw decomposes  , and this value is often associated with the inverse rate of decline.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The cellulose and hemicellulose of straw are easily decomposed, while lignin is not easily decomposed.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The crystalline nature of cellulose, the water repellency of lignin, and the protective layer of the ligninhemicellulose matrix on cellulose  combine to hinder microbial access to the inner regions of the straw.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Structurally diverse plant residues are produced during the decomposition of straw, and these recalcitrant materials accumulate and incorporate into the soil organic matter (SOM).

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Soil water repellency (SWR) increases as water-repellent lignin accumulated from the decomposition of fresh organic matter.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) When water is present on the soil surface, an effect named SWR occurs where the soil is not instantly wet.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) It affects the soil's hydrological balance, water evaporation, erosion, soil infiltration.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Based on Doerr et al., SWR is a transitory attribute of soils that enhances its resistance to wetting and infiltration.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) It is also highly variable in both location and time.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The SWR has an advantageous role in preserving soil stability  and organic carbon sequestration  under specific circumstances.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Further, the SWR intensity and persistence impact soil moisture content.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The SWR is produced by the accumulation of hydrophobic compounds that originate from vegetation  or microorganisms  , or by the decomposition of fresh organic matter with low levels of decomposition and humification.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) In the event of weak attractive forces between molecules at the solid/liquid interfaces, SWR occurs naturally when high-energy soil mineral surfaces are covered by thin films of low-energy organic compounds, resulting in the growth of water-repellent films.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) SOM is known to be present as a thin coating over soil mineral particles or as particulate organic matter, both of which may reduce soil wettability, and increase SWR.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The SOM appears to play an essential role in the occurrence of SWR.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) In line with Deurer et al., there is a correlation between the quantity of SWR and the content of SOM.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The main source of SOM is plant residues, and the hydrophobic component of SOM can be traced back to the original plant input.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The hydrophobic compounds in SOM are derived directly from crop residues containing high levels of waxes, aromatic oils, lipids, and lignin, and are usually more resistant to microbial degradation than hydrophilic substances.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) These aromatic and aliphatic carbons from lipids or lignin in SOM are the most important chemical classes causing SWR effects on soil water status, infiltration capacity  , hydraulic conductivity, and water availability of plants  Moderate water repellency is common in soils and its positive effects on soil structure and quality are recognized.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) To protect organic matter as a stabilizing mechanism, water repellency makes soil aggregates more stable.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Given that the soil's structural stability is improved, an increase in soil water repellency indicates an improvement in soil quality.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) As such, it is important to properly assess water repellency, particularly in agricultural soils.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) However, the possible link between plant residue fractions and SWR for different straw return methods is not well known.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Therefore, the objective of this study was to investigate the effects of different straw return methods on soil organic carbon and total nitrogen contents, straw lignin, cellulose, hemicellulose, and straw residues, as well as soil organic carbon and total nitrogen contents and important straw fractions on SWR.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) In this study, we proposed two broader hypotheses: (1) Straw return is beneficial to increase SOC and TN.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Straw residue and its lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose decomposition rates are higher under different straw return treatments.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) (2) The increase in SOC and TN along with the increase in the decomposition rate of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose in straw affect the CA of water droplets with soil and increase the SWR.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) To test our hypothesis, this study investigated the direct effect of crop residual lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose on SWR and the extent of SWR under different straw-returning strategies, using typical black soils (Argiudolls) and maize stover as reference.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Understanding the dynamics of the interaction between SOC, straw composition, and SWR under different straw-returning practices is essential for managing and predicting soil organic matter and soil quality.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) It also provides a theoretical basis for the effects of different straw-returning methods on the straw decomposition process and soil physicochemical properties.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The SWR was explored using an assortment of methods, notably WDPT (water drop penetration time), MED (ethanol droplet molarity), and CA (contact angle).

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) According to the study by Leelamanie et al., the two most common methods for characterizing SWR are CA and WDPT, with the former related to the level of SWR and the latter to its persistence.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The experiment was conducted at the Experimental Station of Jilin Agricultural University in Changchun, Jilin Province, Northeast China (43 • 48 43.57 N, 125 • 23 38.50 E).

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The area has a humid climate with a mean annual temperature of 4.6 • C and a mean annual precipitation of 600 to 700 mm.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The soil type is a subclass of semi-wet-temperate, semi-alluvial black soils, corresponding to the American systematic classification of claydeposited moist soft soils (Argiudolls).

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The experimental plot was 30 m 2 in size, and maize was grown continuously for 12 years without returning the straw to the field.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The initial organic carbon content was 11.2 g kg -1 and the total nitrogen content was 1.3 g kg-1 as determined by the experiment.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The corn straw was collected from the experimental field of Jilin Agriculture University, in September 2020.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The basic properties of the straw were organic carbon 376.4 g kg-1 , total N 7.22 g kg -1 , total P 7.7 g kg -1 , total potassium 4.5 g kg-1 , and C/N ratio of 61.8.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The nylon mesh bag (manufacturer: Ju feng Net, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China) had a pore size of 0.15 mm (10 cm × 10 cm), allowing water, soil microorganisms, and randomized soil particles to enter.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The field nylon bag burial trial was initiated on 20 April 2021.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Four treatments were set up: 1 control (CK), nylon mesh bags with 10 g of straw were placed on the surface with polyethylene film between the nylon bags and the soil, with no contact with the soil, with the aim to compare with other treatments; 2 straw mulching (CM), nylon mesh bags with 10 g of straw were placed on the soil surface, with the aim to simulate straw mulching in the field; 3 straw deep burial (CD), nylon mesh bags with 10 g of straw were buried 40 cm from the soil surface, with the aim to simulate the deep turning of straw in the field; 4 doubled straw deep burial (CE), nylon mesh bags with 30 g of straw in a nylon mesh bag at 40 cm of soil depth, with the aim to simulate the deep turning of a doubled amount of straw in the field.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Fifteen micro-zones were set up with a micro-zone area of 1 m 2 and each micro-zone consisted of four treatments arranged in randomized groups with three replications of each treatment.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Nylon bags and soil samples were collected at 0, 30, 90, 180, 270, and 360 days after the start of the experiment in each of the three micro-zones for each treatment.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Soil samples were collected at a depth of 5 cm at the interface between the nylon mesh bags and the soil to remove any visible organic debris and stones.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Soil Carbon and Nitrogen Content SOC was determined using the K 2 Cr 2 O 7 -H 2 SO 4 oxidation method.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Soil TN content was determined using the Kjeldahl method.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Lignin: titration with ammonium ferrous sulphate solution; cellulose: titration with ammonium ferrous sulphate solution; hemicellulose: determination by copper iodide.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The contact angle (CA) of the treated soil sample with water was measured at room temperature with a fully automatic contact angle meter (Optical Contact Angle Meter, OCA20, Dataphysics, Filderstadt, Germany).

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Digital micrographs of horizontal views of the water droplets were taken at 0, 1, 3, and 5 s. The CA was measured at five different locations on each surface and the average obtained CA was the final static water CA.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Straw decomposition rate: straw was set at 0, 30, 90, 180, 270, and 360 days after the experimental set-up, to exclude the effect of water content on strawweight, so after washing the straw and air-drying and weighing it (weighing with an electronic balance with an accuracy class of milligrams), a portion of the straw was weighed and dried at 105 • C for 2 h until there was no change in weight and then the water content of the straw was measured, and the dry weight of all the straw was calculated from the water content and measured by subtracting the difference with the weight of the straw at 0 d Straw residue.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Statistical analysis: Data were processed using Microsoft Office Excel 2017 (Microsoft Windows, Redmond, DC, USA) and analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS software (IBM Statistics 21.0, New York, NY, USA) to evaluate the effect of different straw return patterns on all measured soil parameters.

(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) The least significant difference test of p < 0.05 was used to evaluate significant differences in the means of straw return patterns and TUKEYs were adjusted at p < 0.05.
(title:Deep Straw Burial Accelerates Straw Decomposition and Improves Soil Water Repellency) Graphs were compiled using Origin 2021b software (OriginLab Inc., Northampton, MA, USA).
